articles.title: The Boss May Come Today
articles.dek: On a frozen island in 1916, twenty-two stranded men rolled up their sleeping bags every morning for a rescue that seemed never to come. Peter wrote to Christians who were waiting in much the same way.
articles.quote: Every day the Lord seems late is another day his patience is holding the door open for someone still on the way home.
articles.body:
On a narrow strip of rock called Elephant Island, at the frozen edge of Antarctica, twenty-two men lived for more than four months under two upturned lifeboats. Their ship, the Endurance, had been crushed by pack ice and had sunk into the Weddell Sea. They ate seal and penguin, burned blubber for warmth, and slept in reindeer-skin bags that never quite dried. In April 1916 their leader, Ernest Shackleton, climbed into a third small boat, the James Caird, with five companions and set out across roughly 1,300 kilometres of some of the roughest ocean on earth to get help. Before he left, he promised the men he would come back for them.

Weeks went by, and then months. Shackleton's second-in-command, Frank Wild, started a habit the men remembered for the rest of their lives. Every morning he rolled up his sleeping bag and called out, in words several of them later recorded, "Lash up and stow, boys, the Boss may come today." Some of the men grumbled at him. A few had quietly begun to suspect that the Boss had drowned somewhere in the Southern Ocean and that no one would ever come.

From their beach, they had no way of seeing the rest of the story. Shackleton had reached South Georgia, crossed its uncharted mountains on foot, and staggered into a whaling station in May. He then spent the whole southern winter trying to get back to them. A British whaler was turned back by the ice. A Uruguayan trawler failed, and so did a chartered schooner. On the fourth attempt, aboard a small Chilean navy tug called the Yelcho under Captain Luis Pardo, he finally broke through. On August 30, Shackleton stood in a rowing boat off the beach and shouted to ask whether everyone was well. The answer came back across the water: "All safe, all well!" Every one of the twenty-two had survived.

The Apostle Peter wrote his second letter to people standing on a beach of their own. He was an old man by then and knew his time was short: "I know that I will soon put aside the tent of this body" (2 Peter 1:14). His readers were scattered Christians, about a generation after Jesus had promised to return. The apostles who had walked with Jesus were dying one by one, and nothing in the sky had changed. Into that silence came a group Peter calls scoffers, people who mocked the promise and used the long wait as their proof. "They will say, 'Where is this "coming" he promised? Ever since our ancestors died, everything goes on as it has since the beginning of creation'" (2 Peter 3:4).

It is a persuasive argument, and it still is. The sun keeps rising, and so do the bills, while the headlines keep getting worse and the prayer you have prayed for ten years sits unanswered. Peter does not wave the argument away. He reminds his readers that the same word of God that formed the world once judged it in the flood (2 Peter 3:5–6), so a long stretch of calm proves nothing. Then he says what he most wants them to remember: "With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day" (2 Peter 3:8). He is echoing Moses, who prayed, "A thousand years in your sight are like a day that has just gone by" (Psalm 90:4). God lives outside our calendar. What feels endless to us is a breath to him, and he can also pack a lifetime's purpose into a single day.

Then comes the verse that turns the whole complaint around.

"The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance." (2 Peter 3:9)

The Greek words Peter chooses are worth a closer look. The word for "slow" is bradynō, the word for someone who dawdles, someone late because he doesn't care enough to hurry. That is how the scoffers saw God. For God himself, Peter uses makrothymeō, built from makros (long) and thymos (temper or passion). It describes someone who keeps his anger a long way off and takes a deep breath before he acts. The passage turns on a single contrast, and Peter states it plainly: the scoffers called the delay neglect, and Peter calls it mercy.

The phrase that surprises most readers is "patient with you." Peter is writing to believers. The patience he describes is aimed at the church, at the people waiting, at the very ones who were tempted to give up. The delay has a face, and it looks a lot like ours. A few verses later he puts it even more directly: "Bear in mind that our Lord's patience means salvation" (2 Peter 3:15). If the Lord had returned on the morning the scoffers first laughed, you and I would never have been born, much less heard his name. Every century of waiting has been a century of people coming home.

Here the island story gives us a picture and then falls short of it, which is useful too. Shackleton's delay came from his limits: ice, weather, and borrowed ships that couldn't push through. God has no such limits. His delay is chosen, and it comes from the same love that will one day bring him back. From the beach, the waiting felt like silence. On the other side of the water, it was a rescuer giving everything to reach them. Peter wants us to believe the same about our own long waits.

That changes how we use the time we are given. Peter asks, "What kind of people ought you to be? You ought to live holy and godly lives as you look forward to the day of God and speed its coming" (2 Peter 3:11–12). The word for "speed," speudō, means to hurry something along with eager effort. Waiting, for Peter, is active. It looks like Frank Wild rolling up his bedroll on a morning when there was no ship in sight, because the promise was enough reason to be ready. Filipino families know this kind of readiness well. When a parent working abroad is finally coming home, the house is cleaned days ahead, the favorite dish is planned, and someone keeps checking the arrival board long before the plane can possibly land.

Peter spells out what that readiness looks like in everyday life: "make every effort to be found spotless, blameless and at peace with him" (2 Peter 3:14). Being at peace with him includes the quarrel you have been putting off settling, the apology you keep rehearsing and never giving, and the small dishonesty you have learned to live with. Peter closes his letter, and his whole ministry, with a gentle command: "But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (2 Peter 3:18). The waiting years are meant to be growing years, and none of them are wasted.

Tonight, before you sleep, you could do your own small version of lashing up and stowing. Settle one thing you would not want left undone if the Lord came tomorrow, and then pray by name for one person you love who has not yet come home to God. That person may be the very reason the wait has lasted this long. Every day the Lord seems late is another day his patience is holding the door open for someone still on the way home.

The men on Elephant Island were rescued because someone who loved them refused to stop trying to reach them. Our rescuer has never stopped either. Keep your bags packed and your heart at peace, and carry Peter's reminder into the morning: his patience means salvation, perhaps for someone you love and perhaps for you. One day the waiting will be over, and the answer heard across the water will be "all safe, all well."

articles.title: The Gate You Don't Go Back Through
articles.dek: Buried among Ezekiel's measurements is a rule for festival crowds. Read closely, it shows what a meeting with God is supposed to do to us: send us forward, into people we would never have met.
articles.quote: Every meeting with God is meant to carry you straight ahead, out the far gate and into the lives of people you would otherwise never have passed.
articles.body:
Off the reefs of Palawan and the Visayas, in water too deep and dark for most divers, lives a creature whose family line stretches back hundreds of millions of years. The chambered nautilus is a soft-bodied cousin of the squid tucked inside a striped, coiled shell, and Filipino fishermen have pulled those shells up in their nets for generations. Cut one in half and you find something lovely: a spiral of pearly rooms, each a little larger than the last, like the inside of a winding staircase.

Most people never learn how those rooms get there. The nautilus lives only in the newest, outermost chamber. As it grows, it slowly moves its body forward and builds a thin wall of shell behind itself, sealing off the room it has just left, and it never goes back. The old chambers still have work to do. A slender cord of living tissue called the siphuncle runs back through every sealed room, and the animal uses it to adjust the gas and fluid inside them so it can rise and sink through the sea. The places it has outgrown are what keep it afloat. In 1858 the American poet Oliver Wendell Holmes was so moved by this that he wrote, "Build thee more stately mansions, O my soul," a line generations of students have since memorized.

I thought of that small, patient animal while reading one of the most overlooked rules in the Bible. It sits in the last chapters of Ezekiel, among measurements and offerings that most readers skim on their way to somewhere else. Among the cubits and grain offerings is a traffic instruction for worshipers, and it may be one of the warmest pieces of human wisdom in the whole book.

Ezekiel was a priest who never got to serve in the temple he was trained for. He was carried off to Babylon as a young man, and in exile he heard from far away that Jerusalem had fallen and Solomon's temple had burned. Then, "in the twenty-fifth year of our exile" (Ezekiel 40:1), around 573 BC, God gave him a vision of a restored temple, measured down to the thickness of its walls. Chapters 45 and 46 describe how life would work around that holy place. Land is set aside for the priests, the Levites and the prince. The rulers are rebuked in strong words: "You have gone far enough, princes of Israel! Give up your violence and oppression and do what is just and right" (Ezekiel 45:9). Even the market is reformed, with a command to "use accurate scales" (45:10). God is rebuilding a whole society, and how people treat one another sits right beside how they worship.

Then comes the festival day. Picture the great pilgrim feasts, when the whole nation pressed toward the temple courts at once. Families came up from the north and from the south, carrying lambs and baskets of flour, with children riding on their fathers' shoulders. In a crowd that size, people would naturally enter through the nearest gate, worship, turn around, and leave the way they came. God gives a different instruction.

"When the people of the land come before the LORD at the appointed festivals, whoever enters by the north gate to worship is to go out the south gate; and whoever enters by the south gate is to go out the north gate. No one is to return through the gate by which they entered, but each is to go out the opposite gate." (Ezekiel 46:9)

On one level this is plain crowd control. Anyone who has squeezed through Quiapo during the Feast of the Black Nazarene, or tried to leave a packed mall the night before Christmas, knows what happens when thousands of people push in and out of the same door. A one-way flow keeps people from being crushed. The Hebrew adds a lovely layer. The word behind "opposite" comes from nokhach, meaning "in front of" or "straight ahead." A fair way to read it is that worshipers were to keep walking forward, so that nobody met God and then simply retraced their own footsteps home.

One way to read this is that the gate rule also changes who you meet. If you leave through the gate you came in by, you walk home beside the same neighbors, down the same road, past the same faces. If you must leave by the opposite gate, you cross the whole court and pass through the stream of people who arrived from the other end of the country. The farmer from the northern hills brushes shoulders with the shepherd from the southern villages, and each family comes out into a part of the city it did not walk through that morning. In this design, worship ends with you among strangers, heading somewhere new.

The very next verse makes the point more personal: "The prince is to be among them, going in when they go in and going out when they go out" (Ezekiel 46:10). That line would have startled Ezekiel's first readers. Israel's kings had built their palace so close to the temple that God complained, "When they placed their threshold next to my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts... they defiled my holy name" (Ezekiel 43:8). The old rulers kept a private entrance. In the restored city the prince walks in the same crowd, through the same gates, at the same pace as everyone else.

Centuries later, Jewish teachers preserved a tender custom along the same lines. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish tradition written down around AD 200, describes how pilgrims entering the Temple Mount walked around it to the right. Mourners walked around to the left, against the flow of the crowd. When people coming the other way asked what had happened and heard, "I am a mourner," they answered with a blessing: "May he who dwells in this house comfort you" (Mishnah Middot 2:2). The walk was arranged so that the hurting would be seen, met face to face, and blessed by the very people heading the other way.

Put Ezekiel's gates beside that ancient custom and a picture emerges of what meeting God is meant to do to us. Worship turns us outward and forward. Every meeting with God is meant to carry you straight ahead, out the far gate and into the lives of people you would otherwise never have passed. Like the nautilus, we leave the room where we met him and move ahead, and the room we left becomes part of what holds us up. The Sunday service, the early morning prayer and the quiet minutes you spend with this reading are real rooms with God, and each of them is meant to send you out by a different gate into a different crowd.

Most of us have a well-worn route out of church and out of prayer. We greet the same three friends at the door, sit at the same table at the fellowship lunch, and head back into the circle of people who already understand us. Those friendships are gifts from God, and they are worth keeping. Ezekiel's opposite gate simply invites a small, holy detour. This week, after you worship, you might cross the room to the person who always leaves alone, sit beside the new family whose names you have never asked, or message the coworker who has seemed heavy lately. You might ask, as those ancient pilgrims did, "Kumusta ka talaga?" and wait long enough to hear the real answer.

The prince's example belongs here too. Many of us carry a little authority, as a parent, a manager, a small-group leader, or the ate or kuya everyone in the family turns to. Every leader is tempted to want a private door, a way to arrive late, slip out early and stay above the crowd. God's picture of good leadership is a prince who goes in when the people go in and goes out when they go out. Walking at their pace, through their gate, is how a leader learns what the people are carrying.

If you are the one walking against the flow right now, carrying a grief nobody has asked about, take heart from that old custom on the Temple Mount. God arranged his house so that the mourner would be met, and he still puts people in your path, coming from the other side of the court and ready to speak a blessing over you. Let someone ask, and let them comfort you.

The nautilus never returns to a chamber it has outgrown, yet it carries every one of those rooms with it, and they keep it rising in the dark water. Your times with God work the same way, because each one becomes part of what holds you up even as it sends you forward. When you close this page today, walk out the far gate. Somewhere on the other side is a face you would never have passed if you had gone home the way you came, and God may have sent you there for exactly that person.

articles.title: Olive Shoots Around the Table
articles.dek: Psalm 128 pictures a blessed home as an old olive tree ringed by young shoots. A Danish carpenter's late-night lesson to his son shows how the root gets passed on.
articles.quote: What we honor in hidden places becomes the root our children grow from, and the table is where that root reaches them.
articles.illustration: Ole Kirk Christiansen's three-coat varnished ducks
articles.body:
In the early 1930s, in the small Danish village of Billund, a carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen was running out of reasons to hope. The Great Depression had dried up orders for the houses and furniture he built, and farmers around him had no money for new barns. In 1932 his wife died, leaving him alone with four young sons. So Ole did what resourceful people do in a hard season. He looked at the scraps of wood in his workshop and started making things a struggling family could still afford, stepladders and ironing boards at first, and then, more and more, wooden toys.

One of his best sellers was a painted wooden duck that waddled when a child pulled it on a string. One day his son Godtfred, still a boy, came to him pleased with himself. He had saved the business some money, he explained, by giving a batch of ducks two coats of varnish instead of the usual three. Ole did not praise him. He sent the boy back to the railway station to collect the crate, and Godtfred stayed up through the night putting on the third coat. Years later he said he never forgot that night. His father's motto, later carved onto a wooden plaque for the workshop wall, read Det bedste er ikke for godt: only the best is good enough.

Ole called the little company LEGO, from the Danish leg godt, "play well." A fire burned the factory to the ground in 1942, and he rebuilt it. Godtfred grew up to lead the firm and steered it toward the plastic interlocking brick that children around the world now step on barefoot in the dark. Nearly a century later, the company is still owned by the same family. What carried across all those years was a man's character, handed to his son one long night with a varnish brush.

Psalm 128 is a song about that kind of inheritance. It belongs to the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134), a small hymnbook that Israelite pilgrims sang as they walked uphill toward Jerusalem for the great feasts. Picture whole families on the road for days, children riding on their fathers' shoulders, grandparents setting the pace, everyone singing together as the city came into view. The psalm just before it warns that "unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1). Psalm 128 then steps inside a house God has built and lets us look around.

It begins, "Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in obedience to him" (Psalm 128:1). The Hebrew word for blessed is ashre, the same word that opens Psalm 1. It describes a life that is going well, a person whose path is straight and whose days are flourishing. The "fear of the LORD" is the Bible's phrase for a reverent awe of God that shapes how you live, the kind of deep respect that changes your choices when no one is watching. Then the song moves from the road into the home, to work and marriage and children and a shared meal.

"You will eat the fruit of your labor; blessings and prosperity will be yours. Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table." (Psalm 128:2–3)

Every farmer in ancient Israel knew exactly what olive shoots looked like. The olive is a patient tree. A young one can take years to give a real harvest, and a mature tree may keep bearing for centuries. Olive trees also do something at their base that most of us have never seen. Young shoots spring up around the foot of an old trunk, rising from the same root system. If the old trunk is cut down, or killed by frost or fire, those shoots can grow into new trees, so that an orchard lives on for generations from roots far older than anything above the ground. Some of the twisted olive trees in the Garden of Gethsemane are thought to have regrown this way, new trunks rising from very old roots.

The Hebrew word here, shetilim, means young plantings or shoots. One way to read verse 3, then, is this: the children around the table are drawing life from the same root as the parent. What they become depends a great deal on what flows up through that root. The psalmist places them "around your table," and in a home the table is where the sap travels. The phrase "within your house" is even more intimate in Hebrew. It literally means the innermost parts of the house, the private rooms where guests seldom go. The blessing of this psalm grows in hidden places, in the ordinary hours that no visitor sees.

That is why the story of the varnished ducks matters. Godtfred learned his father's root at a workbench late at night, in a moment that had nothing to do with speeches. Children absorb what we treat as important when we assume nobody will check. The fear of the LORD in verse 1 is the root, the honest work of verse 2 is its first fruit, and the table of verse 3 is where it reaches the next generation. What we honor in hidden places becomes the root our children grow from, and the table is where that root reaches them.

Filipinos already understand the table in our bones. We know the long Sunday lunch at Lola's house, the call of "Kain na!" across the yard, and the habit of serving the elders first. Our hapag-kainan is where we learned who we are, what we laugh at, what we pray for, and how we speak of people who are absent. The psalm invites us to see that same table as holy ground, a place where faith is passed down one meal at a time through how we give thanks, how we talk about our work, and how we treat the one who arrives late.

Some who read this will feel a quiet ache. Perhaps there is no spouse at your table, or no children, or the chairs that used to be full are empty now. The psalm's picture is drawn from an Israelite household, but its truth reaches wider. Paul had no children of his own, yet he called Timothy "my true son in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2). Your shoots may be nieces and nephews, the students you teach, the young staff you supervise, or the teenager at church who watches how you handle disappointment. Anyone who eats at your table, or simply learns from your life, is drawing from your root.

The psalm also has hope for families that have known loss. Ole Kirk Christiansen buried his wife and watched his workshop burn, and still the shoots grew. An olive orchard survives the fall of a trunk because the life was always in the root. In verses 5 and 6 the song turns from promise into prayer, as the pilgrims bless one another on the road: "May the LORD bless you from Zion" (Psalm 128:5). The flourishing comes from God. Our part is to stay rooted in him and keep the table open.

Tonight, as you sit down to eat, you might set your phone aside long enough to give thanks out loud and to ask the youngest person present about their day. Tomorrow, when a small task tempts you to skip the third coat, you could do it properly anyway, as an offering to the Lord who sees the innermost rooms. Little by little, roots like that hold a family together across the years, and you may live to hear the psalm's final prayer answered over your own life: "May you see your children's children" (Psalm 128:6).

articles.title: Seven Words from Underground
articles.dek: A scrap of paper from deep inside a Chilean mountain gave a nation new hope. Proverbs 25:25 says good news from far away can do that for a weary soul, and the gospel is the farthest-traveled news of all.
articles.quote: The gospel is cold water from a distant country, and the One who sent it walked the whole distance to bring it himself.
articles.body:
On August 22, 2010, a drill bit came up out of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile after boring nearly 700 meters into the rock. For seventeen days, thirty-three miners had been trapped below the collapsed San José mine near Copiapó, and much of the world had quietly assumed the worst. Their families refused to. They had pitched tents beside the mine entrance and named the place Campamento Esperanza, Camp Hope, and they waited there through dusty days and cold desert nights for any word at all.

When the rescuers pulled up the probe, they found a scrap of paper taped to it, written in red ink. It read, in Spanish, "Estamos bien en el refugio los 33": "We are well in the shelter, the 33." Chile's president, Sebastián Piñera, held the note up before the cameras, and Camp Hope erupted. Mothers wept, strangers embraced, and car horns sounded in cities hundreds of kilometers away. The miners were still trapped deep in the mountain, and it would be almost two more months before the last of them rode the narrow Fénix capsule to the surface on October 13. Yet the families slept differently that night, because the news had reached them before the rescue did.

Filipinos understand that kind of waiting better than most. Millions of our households have a mother working in Dubai, a father on a ship somewhere in the Pacific, or a sister nursing in London, and every one of those homes knows the particular silence of a phone that has not rung in a while. We also know the relief of the call that finally comes, with a tired voice saying, "Okay lang ako dito." A few words from far away, and a whole house can breathe again.

The writer of Proverbs knew that feeling too. Chapter 25 opens with a note about where these sayings came from: "These are more proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (Proverbs 25:1). Some two centuries after Solomon, royal scribes gathered and copied his wisdom, much of it shaped as vivid word pictures that say, in effect, "this is like that." Hezekiah's Judah lived under the shadow of Assyria, and news in that world moved only as fast as a runner or a horse could carry it. A family might wait weeks or months to learn whether a son traveling with a caravan, or a husband marching with the army, was alive. Into that world comes a single, beautiful line.

"Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land." (Proverbs 25:25, NIV)

The Hebrew phrase behind "weary soul" is nefesh ayefah. Nefesh is often translated "soul," but its root picture is the throat, the part of a person that feels thirst. Ayef describes someone faint and worn out, the exhaustion of a traveler who has run out of water. David uses the same word when he writes of longing for God "in a dry and parched land where there is no water" (Psalm 63:1). So the proverb describes good news as something the body feels, like the first swallow of cold water after a long walk under the noon sun. A few verses earlier, the same collection says, "Like a snow-cooled drink at harvest time is a trustworthy messenger to the one who sends him" (Proverbs 25:13). In a hot land, people understood cold water as a gift, and they understood good news the same way.

Scripture gives us a picture of exactly this moment in the life of Jacob. For more than twenty years he believed his son Joseph was dead. Then his other sons came home from Egypt with impossible news: "Joseph is still alive! In fact, he is ruler of all Egypt" (Genesis 45:26). At first the old man could not believe it. "But when they told him everything Joseph had said to them, and when he saw the carts Joseph had sent to carry him back, the spirit of their father Jacob revived" (Genesis 45:27). Nothing in Canaan had changed yet, and the famine was still on. But word had come from a distant land, and a weary father came back to life.

One way to read Proverbs 25:25 is as a quiet preview of the whole story of the Bible. The New Testament word for "gospel" is the Greek euangelion, which simply means "good news." The prophets had already been using the Hebrew equivalent: "How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation, who say to Zion, 'Your God reigns!'" (Isaiah 52:7). And on the night Jesus was born, an angel told frightened shepherds, "I bring you good news that will cause great joy for all the people" (Luke 2:10). The good news of the gospel truly comes from a distant land, because it comes from heaven itself.

Here the gospel goes beyond anything the proverb could have imagined. In every other story, the messenger and the one who sends him are two different people: a runner, a letter, a scrap of paper on a drill bit. In the gospel, the One who sent the message also carried it. Paul writes that Christ "came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near" (Ephesians 2:17). The gospel is cold water from a distant country, and the One who sent it walked the whole distance to bring it himself. He crossed from heaven to a manger, from Galilee to a cross, and from the grave back into the morning, where an angel told the grieving women, "He is not here; he has risen, just as he said" (Matthew 28:6).

That Easter news works much like the note from the San José mine. It arrived before every circumstance had been resolved. The disciples still faced persecution, and you and I still face hospital bills, long separations, and the grief that comes to every family eventually. Yet the decisive word has already come up from the depths: Christ is alive, and those who belong to him are safe. In a sense, the miners' message is the believer's message too. The psalmist says, "Whoever dwells in the shelter of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty" (Psalm 91:1). We are well in the shelter, even while the rescue is still being completed.

This has two very practical meanings for an ordinary Tuesday. The first is for the times when you are the weary one. When your nefesh feels parched, when the week has drained you and the silence from heaven feels long, go back to the news before you try to fix your circumstances. Take ten minutes today to read one of the resurrection accounts slowly, perhaps Luke 24, and let it be cold water before it becomes a lesson. The Christian life begins and is sustained by receiving news, and the people at Camp Hope found their strength in a message long before the capsule ever moved.

The second meaning is for the times when you can be the messenger. Someone you love is waiting by a silent phone right now. It may be a parent abroad who has not heard from you in weeks, a friend recovering in the hospital, or an elderly tita who wonders whether anyone remembers her. A short message from you could be the cold water they need today, and it takes less than a minute to send. And if the Lord opens the door, you may also have the joy of passing on the oldest and best news there is: that God has come near to the weary, and that his shelter is open.

The families in the Atacama Desert waited seventeen days for seven words in red ink. You do not have to wait. The good news from the distant land has already arrived, it is addressed to you by name, and you can drink as deeply as you need. Then, with your own thirst relieved, carry a cup to someone else who is still waiting to hear.
